title: The first hymn is to fire
hookLine: a match struck in a dark kitchen. The Rig Veda's very first hymn begins with fire
carry: agni, the fire, carries our offerings to the gods
last: THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: THE TORCH HELD STILL.

lines: A MATCH IN A DARK KITCHEN.
cards: Before dawn, in a dark kitchen, someone strikes a match. The scratch, the little flare, the smell of it. They touch it to a lamp's wick, or to the burner under the morning's tea, and the room changes.
Faces appear. The kettle appears. The day has started.
Fire is often the first thing awake in a house. So maybe it's no surprise where the Rig Veda begins. Not with a law, a list, or the making of the world.
Its first hymn opens with a single name: Agni. The fire. Today, a new stretch of the path: the Vedas themselves.

teach.b: Start with the name. In the Sanskrit dictionaries, rig is a verse of praise, and veda is knowing. So the Rig Veda is knowledge carried in verses of praise.
It's not a story told start to finish, and it's not a book of rules.
It's a collection of hymns, made to be chanted aloud, addressed to many gods. And it opens with fire.

In paraphrase, the first line says: I praise Agni, the household priest set in front, the god of the offering, the one who calls the gods, the richest giver of treasure. Notice the jobs piled onto one flame.
Agni is the fire on the altar. He's the priest at the ritual. He calls out to the other gods and carries the offering up to them.
Fire is the go-between, where earth and heaven meet. The next verse says seers old and new praise him. And the last verse turns tender.

teach.h: EASY TO REACH, AS A FATHER IS.
teach.b: Be easy to reach, it asks Agni, as a father is to his son. Stay with us, for our good. That's why fire still stands at the heart of so many Hindu rites.
In a havan, ghee and grain go into the flame, because Agni carries the offering to the gods. At a Hindu wedding, the couple walks around the sacred fire, with Agni as witness.
And in many homes, a lamp is lit and waved before the deity at aarti. At the start of the Vedas, fire is the go-between. It still is.

how: The Rig Veda's hymns are chanted rather than read silently, and fire remains central to Hindu ritual: a fire is kindled at weddings and in the havan, and lamps are waved before deities in worship.

games.q: what does “what the rig veda is” mean?
o: a book of laws for kings and their households
one long story of how the gods made the world
a collection of hymns of praise, made to be chanted

games.q: the first hymn — tap the pairs.
p: be easy to reach, as a father is

s: the Rig Veda is mainly a book of rules
it's a collection of hymns of praise, made to be chanted, addressed to many gods.
the Rig Veda's first hymn is to Agni, the fire
it opens: I praise Agni, the household priest, the god of the offering.
in the first hymn, Agni is distant and hard to approach
its last verse asks him to be easy to reach, as a father is to his son.

games.q: at a Hindu wedding, the couple walks around a sacred fire. going back to the Rig Veda's first hymn, why fire?
o: Agni is the go-between of people and gods, there as witness.
the fire is there to keep the guests warm.
fire is just decoration for the photos.
games.why: from the very first hymn, Agni is the priest who calls the gods and carries the offering. many families speak of Agni as the witness to the vows.

practice: If it's safe, light a diya, a small oil lamp, or a candle; if not, picture one. Many Hindu homes light a lamp like this at dawn or dusk.
Watch the flame for a while, then offer something small into its light, a thank-you or a name you're holding, the way an offering goes into the havan fire.
If you pray, greet Agni, or the deity you love, as one who is easy to reach.

wordCard.voice: What the Rig Veda is. Knowledge in verses of praise, a collection of hymns made to be chanted, opening with a hymn to Agni, the fire.

orig.note: Sanskrit: from rich, a verse of praise, and veda, knowing. The name of the collection of hymns.

carryVoice: Your line: agni, the fire, carries our offerings to the gods. The Rig Veda's very first hymn asks that flame to stay close. Rest well.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 1.1.1 (I praise Agni, the household priest, god of the sacrifice, the invoker, richest bestower of treasure)
